paragraphs: Managing a shared resource involves more than achieving good average control performance. Multiple decision makers can have incentives that produce undesirable collective outcomes, as illustrated by the tragedy of the commons. This paper studies that issue for networked systems whose controllers are general-purpose reinforcement learning agents, with common-pool resource management as the motivating application.

The authors use empirical game-theoretic analysis to examine how system design affects the resulting strategic solutions. Their focus is the information structure: what agents share, which communication protocol they use, and how the communication network connects them. The agents are engineered systems constrained by resources such as memory, computation, and communication bandwidth, rather than models of biologically evolved human behavior.

The contribution is an additional way to compare multi-agent control systems. Information-sharing choices have consequences for the strategic behavior that emerges, alongside familiar considerations such as efficiency, robustness, scalability, and mean control performance. The analysis therefore makes communication design part of understanding the incentives and operating behavior of a resource-management system.
neurips-2020-a-game-theoretic-analysis-o.tldr: The paper uses empirical game theory to examine how communication design shapes strategic behavior in reinforcement-learning systems managing shared resources.

paragraphs: Cross-validation assesses a model by repeatedly fitting it on different portions of the data, which becomes costly for expensive learning algorithms. Approximate cross-validation aims to obtain similar assessments from a single fit. This paper addresses a difficulty with that shortcut: existing approximations can become both slower and less accurate when the data have many dimensions.

The proposed method exploits approximate low rank, meaning that much of the data's variation can be captured in fewer dimensions. The authors show that the Hessian matrix involved in approximate cross-validation has corresponding low-rank structure. Although the calculation uses its inverse, they establish that an approximation based on the largest eigenvalues can provide fast, reliable results.

A second finding concerns accuracy: with approximately low-rank data, existing approximation errors roughly depend on the smaller effective rank rather than the full dimension. Together, these insights support theoretical quality guarantees and efficiently computed error upper bounds. Experiments on real and simulated datasets demonstrate the method's speed and accuracy, and the usefulness of those bounds.
neurips-2020-approximate-cross-validatio.tldr: Approximate low-rank structure enables faster, more accurate approximate cross-validation in high dimensions, with computable error bounds.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to learn tasks one after another while retaining what it learned previously. The authors argue that placing different tasks in a shared vector space creates interference, even when methods use stored examples, parameter penalties, or expanding networks to reduce forgetting. Their proposal changes the geometry in which tasks are represented.

Each task is learned in a separate low-rank subspace, and these subspaces are kept orthogonal to one another. The aim is to reduce interference by separating the directions associated with different tasks. The method also learns isometric mappings so that gradients coming from those subspaces remain orthogonal. It formulates network training as optimization over the Stiefel manifold to impose this geometric structure.

The authors report strong results relative to an experience-replay baseline on standard continual-learning classification benchmarks, including settings with and without memory. These findings support orthogonal task representations as a useful approach to reducing interference. The stated goal is to minimize interference while preserving learning across the task sequence.
neurips-2020-continual-learning-in-low-r.tldr: The method separates sequential tasks into low-rank orthogonal subspaces and preserves gradient orthogonality to reduce interference.

paragraphs: Data Diversification improves neural machine translation by changing the training data available to the final model. Multiple models translating in forward and backward directions generate predictions, which are combined with the original dataset. A final translation model then learns from this expanded collection of translation examples.

The approach is presented as applicable to all neural machine translation models. It does not require the additional monolingual data used by back-translation, and the final model avoids the extra parameters and computation associated with running an ensemble. The multiple models contribute through preparation of the training data, allowing their predictions to influence a single final translator.

The authors report BLEU scores of 30.7 and 43.7 on the WMT'14 English–German and English–French tasks, described as state of the art. They also report substantial gains on eight other tasks, including low-resource translation. Their comparisons favor diversification over knowledge distillation and dual learning. A reported tradeoff between perplexity and BLEU shows that improving translation scores need not coincide with improving the model's probabilistic fit.
neurips-2020-data-diversification-a-simp.tldr: Training on original data combined with predictions from multiple translation models improves translation quality without requiring an ensemble at inference.

paragraphs: Optimizing several competing objectives requires choosing evaluations that reveal useful tradeoffs without spending too many samples. Bayesian optimization uses an acquisition function to guide that choice, but strong acquisition functions can themselves be expensive to optimize. This paper targets Expected Hypervolume Improvement, whose computational demands have made its use challenging.

The authors derive qEHVI for selecting multiple candidate points jointly, including settings with constraints. Its calculation gives the joint expected improvement of the candidate batch, up to Monte Carlo integration error. Crucially, automatic differentiation supplies exact gradients of that Monte Carlo estimator. This distinction matters: the gradients are exact for the estimator, while the expectation still involves sampling error.

Those gradients allow first-order and quasi-second-order optimization methods to search for useful candidate batches. The formulation also takes advantage of modern programming tools and hardware acceleration. The empirical evaluation finds qEHVI computationally practical in many scenarios and reports better performance than state-of-the-art multi-objective Bayesian optimization algorithms at a fraction of their wall time.
neurips-2020-differentiable-expected-hyp.tldr: qEHVI makes joint, constrained multi-objective candidate selection practical by differentiating its Monte Carlo estimator and using hardware acceleration.

paragraphs: Compressing BERT to one fixed size can leave a deployment poorly matched to devices with different memory and computation budgets. DynaBERT instead builds a model whose width and depth can be selected to adjust its size and latency. A single trained model therefore supports multiple smaller subnetworks for different efficiency requirements.

Training proceeds in two stages. First, the model learns to operate at different widths. It then learns to vary both width and depth, transferring knowledge from the full-sized model into the smaller subnetworks. Network rewiring arranges important attention heads and neurons so that they are shared by more of those subnetworks, helping preserve useful components across size choices.

Experiments under different efficiency constraints show that the largest dynamic BERT and RoBERTa configurations perform comparably to their respective base models. At smaller widths and depths, the proposed models consistently outperform the existing BERT compression methods tested. The results support adaptive sizing as a way to serve varied hardware budgets while maintaining competitive task performance.
neurips-2020-dynabert-dynamic-bert-with-.tldr: DynaBERT trains shared subnetworks with adjustable width and depth to deliver competitive performance across different deployment budgets.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to maintain a valuable subset when available items keep changing. The objective is monotone and submodular: adding items does not decrease value, and additional items have diminishing returns. A cardinality constraint limits the chosen subset to at most k elements. This selection problem appears in applications such as summarization, recommendation, and data subset selection.

The authors introduce a dynamic algorithm that handles both insertions and deletions from the available ground set. With high probability, it maintains a solution worth at least a fraction one-half minus epsilon of the current optimum over a sequence of updates. The guarantee is approximate, allowing efficient maintenance without requiring an exact optimal subset after each change.

For z updates, the total running time is O(k²z epsilon⁻³ log⁵ n), where n is the largest ground-set size encountered. Consequently, the average cost per update is O(k² epsilon⁻³ log⁵ n). The result provides a formal combination of solution quality and update efficiency, with only a polylogarithmic dependence on the ground-set size.
neurips-2020-dynamic-submodular-maximiza.tldr: A dynamic algorithm maintains a near-half-optimal submodular selection with high probability as items are inserted and deleted.

paragraphs: Data with multiple categorical fields can contain heterogeneous groups whose differences appear within the categories of a field. Fitting one universal model to all these groups can demand considerable complexity. This paper proposes field-wise learning, using the data's existing organization to fit simpler models that respond to category-specific differences.

The proposed approach uses field-focused linear models with variance and low-rank constraints. The constraints are intended to improve generalization and reduce the number of parameters while retaining the ability to capture variation between groups. Because the models are organized around fields, their learned behavior can also be interpreted at that level.

The authors provide theory that could help explain how overparameterization affects their model's generalization, and that supports the variance constraints used during learning. Experiments on two large-scale datasets report superior performance, illustrate the trend predicted by the generalization-error bound, and demonstrate interpretable outcomes. The contribution combines a structured modeling choice with supporting analysis and empirical evidence for learning from high-dimensional categorical data.
neurips-2020-field-wise-learning-for-mul.tldr: Field-wise learning uses constrained, category-sensitive linear models to capture heterogeneous categorical data while controlling model complexity.

paragraphs: GANSpace investigates how to turn a generative adversarial network's internal variation into understandable image-editing controls. The desired changes include viewpoint, age, lighting, and time of day. Instead of treating image synthesis as an opaque mapping, the method analyzes directions in the generator's latent or feature space that can support meaningful edits.

The central tool is principal component analysis, which identifies prominent directions of variation. The authors then perturb the generator along those directions at particular layers. Choosing where to apply a direction provides many interpretable controls, making the layer of intervention part of the editing mechanism as well as the direction itself.

The paper demonstrates results across different GANs and training datasets, with qualitative matches to edit directions previously obtained through supervised approaches. It also shows that BigGAN can accept layer-wise control in a manner resembling StyleGAN. These findings make a relatively simple statistical analysis useful for exploring generator behavior and constructing controls whose visible effects people can understand.
neurips-2020-ganspace-discovering-interp.tldr: GANSpace uses principal components and layer-wise perturbations to discover understandable controls for generated images.

paragraphs: Metric learning constructs a distance measure for methods such as nearest-neighbor classification. This paper asks how the optimization procedure, especially its number of training iterations, affects performance beyond the training data. It develops learning guarantees for non-convex metric-learning objectives optimized with gradient descent, making training duration part of the theoretical account.

The analysis identifies a generalization PAC bound as a sufficient condition for agnostic PAC learnability. It obtains this bound through uniform convergence over a densely concentrated part of parameter space. For gradient-descent-trained classifiers, the authors give generalization guarantees when both the classifier and loss satisfy Lipschitz smoothness conditions, and show that fewer iterations can improve the guarantee.

The paper translates these findings into SMILE, a method designed to satisfy the required smoothness property. SMILE combines metric learning with representative-instance learning and uses early stopping during gradient descent. Its design aims for better discrimination and lower nearest-neighbor computation costs. The result connects an explicit regularity assumption and iteration-dependent theory to concrete choices in a learning algorithm.
neurips-2020-generalization-bound-of-gra.tldr: Under stated smoothness conditions, iteration-dependent generalization bounds motivate early stopping for non-convex metric learning.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms choose which options to sample using results observed so far. When those data are later used for statistical conclusions, the adaptive collection process complicates inference. This paper studies data collected in batches and develops methods for obtaining dependable tests and confidence intervals from such experiments.

The authors prove that arm-selection probabilities cannot generally be assumed to settle around fixed values. This lack of concentration matters because familiar inference procedures, including conventional asymptotic-normality arguments and the bootstrap, can then produce too many false positives. Their confidence intervals can also cover the true quantity less often than advertised, even in asymptotically large samples.

The proposed Batched Ordinary Least Squares estimator, or BOLS, addresses this problem. The paper proves its asymptotic normality for both multi-arm and contextual bandit data. It also establishes robustness to changes in the baseline reward over time. These properties support reliable Type-1 error control and accurate confidence intervals, connecting adaptive decision-making with subsequent statistical assessment.
neurips-2020-inference-for-batched-bandi.tldr: BOLS enables reliable inference from batched bandit data despite unstable sampling probabilities and changing baseline rewards.

paragraphs: This paper studies generalized linear models in an extremely sparse regime: both the number of nonzero signal entries and the number of observations grow sublinearly with the signal's total size. Its goal is to characterize how much information the observations contain and how accurately a Bayesian estimator can recover the signal as system size grows.

The authors prove a variational expression for asymptotic mutual information per observation. For signal entries drawn from a discrete distribution with finite support, this yields an expression for minimum mean-square error. Under suitable vanishing sparsity and sampling-rate scalings, that error decreases in piecewise-constant steps rather than necessarily improving smoothly.

In specific cases, the behavior becomes all-or-nothing: the asymptotic error drops sharply from its maximum to zero at a critical sampling rate. The analysis extends beyond linear regression to learning perceptron weights with general activation functions in a teacher-student setting. It also discusses a corresponding transition in generalization error with sublinearly many training examples, showing how abrupt learning thresholds can arise in this regime.
neurips-2020-information-theoretic-limit.tldr: The paper characterizes asymptotic information and Bayesian error in sparse generalized linear models, revealing all-or-nothing learning transitions in specific regimes.

paragraphs: A learning system's 3D reconstruction quality depends partly on how it represents shapes. DefTet represents volume using tetrahedral meshes and learns both where mesh vertices belong and which regions are occupied. Adjusting geometry and occupancy together provides a way to describe detailed surfaces and complex topology within a volumetric representation.

The representation is differentiable with respect to standard reconstruction losses, allowing it to participate directly in neural-network training. The authors show that it can represent arbitrary complex topology and produce high-fidelity reconstructions with substantially smaller grids than alternative volumetric approaches. Its predicted geometry already has a tetrahedral mesh representation, avoiding a separate post-processing step to obtain that structure.

The reported results combine reconstruction quality with memory and computational efficiency. DefTet matches or exceeds the quality of previous leading approaches and the performance of the fastest ones considered. Demonstrations include high-quality tetrahedral meshes reconstructed directly from noisy point clouds and high-quality 3D results from a single image. These findings support jointly adapting mesh geometry and occupancy as a useful reconstruction strategy.
neurips-2020-learning-deformable-tetrahe.tldr: DefTet learns vertex positions and occupancy in tetrahedral meshes to produce detailed, efficient 3D reconstructions.

paragraphs: Detecting whether a network has changed might seem easier than learning its entire structure, particularly when only a few connections change. This paper examines that intuition for Ising models. It derives information-theoretic limits on the number of samples needed to detect sparse structural changes, including settings where the underlying network has local sparsity.

The central result is a worst-case, minimax statement: detecting sparse changes can require as many samples as learning the whole model. This challenges the expectation, suggested by earlier sparse-recovery approaches, that the required data should scale only with the number of changed connections. A small change set does not by itself ensure an easier testing problem.

The authors also study edge deletions in forest-structured graphs and high-temperature ferromagnets. In these cases, small-change testing remains similarly difficult, while large-change testing is distinctly easier than structure learning. The findings suggest that tools successful for recovering sparse structures may not transfer directly to change detection, and motivate algorithm development aimed at detecting larger changes.
neurips-2020-limits-on-testing-structura.tldr: Detecting sparse changes in Ising models can be as sample-demanding as learning the whole structure, while larger changes can be easier in studied cases.

paragraphs: Structured pruning reduces neural-network computation by removing entire neurons. One common approach learns scaling factors for neurons and removes those whose factors fall below a threshold. A factor near zero suppresses that neuron's contribution. The paper identifies a drawback of using L1 regularization for this purpose: it pushes every factor downward, including those associated with important neurons.

The proposed polarization regularizer instead encourages a separation between suppressed and retained neurons. The authors prove that it pushes some scaling factors to zero and others toward a positive value. This matches the intended pruning behavior more directly: unimportant neurons are turned off while important ones keep substantial influence on the network's output.

Experiments report substantially better structured-pruning results with polarization than with L1 regularization. On CIFAR and ImageNet, the authors report results described as state of the art. The contribution links a theoretical property of the regularizer to the practical selection decision, giving the pruning process an explicit mechanism for distinguishing neurons to remove from neurons to preserve.
neurips-2020-neuron-level-structured-pru.tldr: Polarization regularization separates neuron scaling factors into zero and positive groups, improving structured pruning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks which available option has the highest reward, with a specified level of confidence. In stochastic linear bandits, the paper's objective is to reach that conclusion using as few samples as possible. Its algorithm is designed to adapt its sampling effort to the difficulty of the particular problem instance.

The sampling rule tracks an optimal allocation of draws across arms. The authors show that this rule can be updated arbitrarily infrequently without losing the stated theoretical guarantees. They also provide a stopping rule that does not depend on the number of arms, distinguishing it from existing identification strategies discussed in the paper.

The algorithm's sample complexity matches known instance-specific lower bounds asymptotically, both almost surely and in expectation. This is a long-run optimality statement rather than an exact finite-sample equality. Experiments suggest substantial improvements over existing algorithms. The paper additionally provides a first analysis of best-arm identification when a linear bandit has a continuous set of arms, extending the theoretical setting beyond a discrete collection of choices.
neurips-2020-optimal-best-arm-identifica.tldr: An allocation-tracking algorithm identifies the best linear-bandit arm with fixed confidence and asymptotically optimal instance-specific sample complexity.

paragraphs: An optimization algorithm can reveal information through the locations it queries, even if its feedback remains private. This paper studies a learner seeking the optimum of a convex function through sequential queries to a stochastic gradient oracle. An adversary sees the query points and tries to infer the learner's result, but cannot observe the oracle's responses.

The learner must balance accurate optimization with making the optimum difficult for that observer to identify. The authors formalize this accuracy–privacy tradeoff through query complexity: how many oracle calls are needed for specified accuracy and privacy levels. They derive lower and upper bounds that describe the cost of satisfying both requirements.

For the lower bounds, the paper develops a general information-theoretic template and applies it to stochastic convex optimization and noisy binary search. It also presents a generic secure learning protocol whose upper bound matches the lower bound up to logarithmic factors. This establishes nearly matching requirements and achievable performance within the stated observation model.
neurips-2020-optimal-query-complexity-of.tldr: The paper nearly characterizes the query cost of accurate optimization when an adversary can observe query locations but not oracle feedback.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with continuous states and actions needs a way to account for how large and complicated those spaces are. This paper considers spaces equipped with a metric, which provides a notion of distance. It revisits an existing algorithm and sharpens the analysis of its regret, the performance loss associated with learning rather than already acting optimally.

The refined guarantee depends on the instance's zooming dimension. This quantity captures the size of the sets of nearly optimal actions, so it focuses on the portions of the problem that contain promising decisions. Earlier analyses used covering dimension, a broader measure of the space's complexity; the abstract states that zooming dimension is always smaller.

The significance is that the guarantee reflects the structure of the particular learning problem instead of relying only on the full space's dimension. The contribution is a refined analysis of an existing algorithm. The authors identify it as the first provably adaptive guarantee for reinforcement learning in metric spaces.
neurips-2020-provably-adaptive-reinforce.tldr: A refined regret analysis makes continuous-space reinforcement-learning guarantees depend on the complexity of nearly optimal actions.

paragraphs: Sound and video often describe the same event while conveying different information about it. Cross-Modal Deep Clustering, or XDC, uses that combination to learn representations without manual labels. The method clusters examples in one modality and uses those group assignments as training supervision for the other modality, allowing audio and vision to guide each other's learning.

The motivation is that predicting information across modalities may be more rewarding than learning entirely within one modality. Shared meaning makes the prediction possible, while differences between sound and images make it useful. Experiments find that XDC outperforms single-modality clustering and other multimodal variants, and achieves leading self-supervised accuracy on multiple audio and video benchmarks.

The strongest reported comparison concerns action recognition. On HMDB51 and UCF101, a video model pretrained with XDC on large-scale unlabeled data significantly outperforms the same architecture pretrained with full supervision on ImageNet and Kinetics. This provides evidence that cross-modal supervision can produce highly effective transferable representations, with the comparison tied to the evaluated architecture, datasets, and tasks.
neurips-2020-self-supervised-learning-by.tldr: XDC trains audio and video representations using each modality's clusters to supervise the other, yielding strong self-supervised action-recognition results.

paragraphs: Children develop expectations about their surroundings early in life, raising a question about how much can be learned from sensory experience through generic learning mechanisms. This paper investigates a narrower part of that question: whether high-level visual representations can emerge from the kinds of visual input young children encounter, using modern self-supervised learning.

The researchers train with a longitudinal video dataset recorded from the viewpoints of three young children. This gives the learning system natural, egocentric visual experience rather than an abstract account of what children might see. They apply generic self-supervised objectives to examine what useful visual structure these methods can extract from developmentally realistic data.

The reported result is the emergence of powerful high-level visual representations from those videos. It supports the capacity of generic self-supervised learning to extract meaningful visual information from this form of experience. The study's scope is the development of visual categories and representations; the broader question of how much early knowledge requires substantive innate biases remains beyond what this investigation addresses.
neurips-2020-self-supervised-learning-th.tldr: Generic self-supervised methods learn strong visual representations from natural videos recorded from three young children's perspectives.

paragraphs: ShapeFlow learns how to deform 3D shapes across a class with substantial variation. A latent vector specifies a continuous movement of an existing source shape toward a target. This makes the learned space a space of transformations, where the source supplies geometric details and the target guides the resulting structural pose.

A neural network parameterizes the continuous flow field that moves the geometry. The approach supports multiple templates, is agnostic to shape topology, and preserves fine geometric detail. The authors show that deformations can be guaranteed to have desirable properties such as one-to-one correspondence, freedom from self-intersections, or volume preservation. These are properties that the flow formulation can support, rather than an assertion that every deformation automatically has all of them.

The paper demonstrates shape generation through deformation, transfer of geometric style, interpolation, and unsupervised learning of consistent parameterizations across shape classes. These applications illustrate why a learned transformation space is useful: it can organize relationships between shapes while retaining meaningful information from the source geometry.
neurips-2020-shapeflow-learnable-deforma.tldr: ShapeFlow learns continuous deformations between 3D shapes, supporting detailed geometry, style transfer, and controllable geometric properties.

paragraphs: Information-theoretic generalization bounds connect a learning algorithm's behavior on new data to how much information its output carries about its training sample. This paper sharpens that approach by considering a larger supersample from which the actual training sample is selected randomly. It measures mutual information conditional on that supersample.

The authors first show that these conditional-information bounds are tighter than corresponding bounds based on unconditional mutual information. They then obtain further improvements by combining reasoning about individual samples with data-dependent analysis, using disintegrated mutual information. The progression refines which information enters the bound, rather than treating all dependence between the output and dataset as a single undifferentiated quantity.

The paper applies these results to Langevin dynamics, a noisy iterative learning algorithm. Conditioning on the supersample makes it possible to use information from the optimization trajectory and derive tighter bounds through hypothesis tests. The contribution is therefore both a hierarchy of stronger generalization guarantees and a demonstration of how an algorithm's training path can improve its analysis.
neurips-2020-sharpened-generalization-bo.tldr: Conditional mutual information yields tighter generalization bounds and lets Langevin-dynamics analyses use information from the optimization trajectory.

paragraphs: SwAV learns image representations without labels by connecting different augmented views of the same image through cluster assignments. It clusters data during training and asks the representation of one view to predict the cluster code assigned to another. This swapped prediction encourages consistent representations without explicitly comparing large numbers of feature pairs.

The online method works with both small and large batches and is designed to scale to unbounded amounts of data. It avoids a large memory bank and a special momentum network, making it more memory efficient than the previous contrastive methods discussed. The paper also introduces multi-crop augmentation, mixing views at different resolutions instead of using only two full-resolution views without increasing memory or computation requirements.

The reported evaluation achieves 75.3% ImageNet top-1 accuracy with ResNet-50. It also surpasses supervised pretraining on every transfer task considered in the paper. These results support cluster-assignment prediction as an effective representation-learning objective, while the memory and augmentation choices address practical costs associated with learning from multiple image views.
neurips-2020-unsupervised-learning-of-vi.tldr: SwAV learns visual features by predicting cluster assignments across image views, achieving strong results with an efficient online training approach.

paragraphs: USADTM combines unsupervised and semi-supervised learning to improve classification when only a few examples have labels. Its central challenge is to extract meaningful structure from unlabeled examples and connect that structure to the actual classes of interest. The framework uses the small labeled set to guide how unlabeled data contribute to training.

First, a Triplet Mutual Information loss supports unsupervised semantic aggregation, producing semantic labels for unlabeled examples. Supervision from labeled data then aligns those labels with real classes. A dynamically updated feature pool storing labeled samples also assigns proxy labels to unlabeled examples, which become targets for cross-entropy training. These mechanisms turn discovered structure and labeled reference information into learning signals.

The authors evaluate the framework on four standard semi-supervised benchmarks and report top performance. On CIFAR-10, the stated accuracies are 90.46% with 40 labels and 95.20% with 250 labels. The findings demonstrate strong classification performance in the evaluated low-label settings, supporting the framework's aim of reducing the amount of manual annotation needed.
neurips-2020-unsupervised-semantic-aggre.tldr: USADTM combines unsupervised semantic grouping and labeled-example guidance to train accurate classifiers with few labeled examples.

paragraphs: A model can encounter several useful features without representing all of them equally. This paper investigates what determines that selection using synthetic datasets where the relevance of individual features can be controlled. The experiments examine both task-relevant and irrelevant information, connecting representation choices to the model's initial state and its training task.

When two features redundantly predict labels, the model favors one, and that preference reflects which feature was more easily decoded linearly before training. Training enhances relevant features and partially suppresses irrelevant ones. In some cases, an easy but weak predictor suppresses a harder, stronger predictor. Models trained on both easy and hard features also resemble models trained only on the easy feature.

Easy features produce more consistent representations across training runs than hard features. The authors additionally find greater representational similarity to an untrained model than to models trained on a different task. Together, these observations show that predictive usefulness alone does not determine what a model represents: initial accessibility, feature difficulty, and task choice all shape the observed outcomes.
neurips-2020-what-shapes-feature-represe.tldr: Controlled experiments show that initial feature accessibility and learning difficulty influence what models represent, sometimes favoring weaker but easier predictors.
